chapter_theme: Songs at Kathirkamam (கதிர்காமம்) in Ilam, the Lord of the hill among waterfalls, fruit trees and monkeys: the poet confesses courting women and flattering patrons, the household that eats up a life, and the hour of Death's torturers, and asks for bhakti, the feet and the stainless state of sayujya; two songs lament a lovesick girl, and two are praise alone.
structure_note: Pure praise (636, with the refrain பெருமாள்காண், and 642, addressed to Murugan and then to Siva); patrons and women (637, 641, 644, 649); the householder (638); bhakti, jnana and the end of the paths (639, 643, 646); akam laments in another's voice (645, 647); Death's men (648); 640 is largely obscure. Murugan is twice identified with Sambandar (639, 641), and 643 names the Thiruppugazh as the gift he gave the poet.

636.reading: A song of praise only, each line closing 'behold the Lord' (பெருமாள்காண்): Murugan is the nephew of Murari with Lakshmi on his chest, the Kumara whose songs fill earth and sky, the emerald-peacock lord who plays in the minds of devotees, the lord of Kathirkamam where waterfalls fling gems and pearls, the hero who ground mountains to dust as the demons died, and the guru of the pure Siva with serpent, crescent and Ganga in his hair. It ends with the lord of the gods and the lover of the hunter girl.
636.nuance: The refrain காண் ('see!') makes the song a pointing-out, as if the poet showed the god to the listener line by line. மருவும் அடியார்கள் மனதில் விளையாடு: the devotees' minds are named as one of his playgrounds, beside the hill and the field. இருவினை இலாத ... இமையவர் are the gods free of the two deeds.

637.reading: The poet heaps abuse on the shameless, civet-scented women without grace who deluded him, and confesses that he sang the praises of great sinners who show no kindness, calling them masters of the arts, Meru, the rain cloud and the wish-tree, tirelessly seeking gifts; he asks Murugan to look on him so that he does not die so. The praise names the vel thrown into the sea at Sura, Murugan as son of the Himalaya's daughter and of the Ganga and the lake, husband of the hunters' daughter and Devayanai, the young one of the old town Kathirkamam.
637.nuance: The patron's praises are given in his own flattering terms (மேரு, பருவமேகம், தரு), the stock comparisons of court poetry, so the confession is also a poet's shame at his craft misused. The opening string of abuse (கலதி, பூத வேதாளி, ஞாளி, கோமாளி) is hard to divide; நீழ்வாடை in the praise is probably நீள்வாடை.

638.reading: The poet counts what a householder needs: cloth to wear, rich food for hunger, water and clothes, remedies for the body's sickness, a young woman within and a house to sleep in; getting all this, he bathes in the sea of delusion as protector of a long line of kin and his life goes in vain, and he asks for the day when Murugan calls him, gives him a mind of grace and the awareness of jnana, and rules him as he whirls in the mountain of births. The praise tells at length how the monkeys were sent searching west, north and east, and Maruti, crossing south, found the lady in the grove and gave Rama's golden ring.
638.nuance: The plea is built of a repeated வேணும் ('one needs'), so the household appears as a list of wants that never ends; the verdict is உயிர் அவமே போம, the life simply wasted. The Ramayana in the praise follows Hanuman rather than Rama, and how it connects to Murugan at Kathirkamam is not clear from the text; the line குறிப்பிற் குறிபோன போதிலும் வரலாமோ is obscure.

639.reading: A short song: the poet asks for matchless bhakti, the thought of the sweet feet morning and evening, and for Murugan to dwell close in the ocean of his heart and shine within him. The praise names the dweller on Kathirkamam hill with arms like golden Meru, whose anklets carry sweet speech, and the Lord who straightened the hump of the Pandya.
639.nuance: வழுதி கூன் நிமிர்த்த: straightening the Pandya king's hump is Sambandar's miracle at Madurai, so Murugan is identified with Sambandar, as in 641, 653 and 666.

640.reading: Much of this song is hard to divide. It seems to praise the hero of Kathirkamam hill, who rides the peacock dancing until the northern peak is powdered, and to confess that the poet does not worship as one of the hereditary kin; it then names Murugan who went to the millet field as the servant of the new maiden of the forest and wearied there, the life of those who make room for the poor, seated on an emerald peacock, and ends: whether one speaks kind words or proud words, the Lord pities the poor.
640.nuance: The close is the clearest line: இதமொழி பகரினும் மதமொழி பகரினும் ஏழைக்கு இரங்கும், grace that does not wait on the right words. அபிநவ குமரி அடிமையாய் புனம் சென்று reverses the usual servitude: the god becomes Valli's servant. The opening lines (கனகத நககுலி புணரித ...) resist division.

641.reading: The poet describes women who stroll the streets like peacocks with eyes like spears, who bring under their bodies' power even those on the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga, deceitful women whom he calls the great snare of death and maya, and asks that Murugan's grace come to him, sunk on their shining bed. The praise names Murugan son of Uma, the Gayatri and Parasakti, who wrote a madal and served by the watch-platform for the hunter girl, the king of poets who freed the gods, and the sun of the Kauniya clan who wept and saved the world, at Kathirkamam.
641.nuance: The women undo even those on the ordered Saiva paths (சரியை க்ரியை யோகத்தின் வழிவருக்கு), so the danger is set above ascetic discipline. அழுது உலகை வாழ்வித்த கவுணிய குலாதித்த is Sambandar, of the Kauniya gotra, who wept as a child and was fed by Uma: Murugan is identified with him. மடலெழுதி: Murugan himself in the lover's extremity, as in 656 and 664. The phrase மகாதத்தை in the plea is uncertain.

642.reading: A song of praise in two parts: first Murugan, born in the reeds, who leapt at Sura, followed him as far as he fled, split his body in two, heaped his heads and chests and won the cock as his banner, with a plea for the lotus feet; then Siva, who laughed and burned the cities when their lords came to fight, flayed and wore the elephant's hide, and burned Madana to charcoal with the look of his brow. It ends with Murugan the pearl of Kathirkamam.
642.nuance: The rhythm is a chain of short past-tense verbs (பொறுத்தார் பரித்தார் சிரித்தார் எரித்தார் ...), each act of Siva one beat. The song closes on முருகோனே, not பெருமாளே.

643.reading: The poet asks whether he will reach the true reality that is beyond the reach of those on the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga, that the divisions of sects cannot approach, beyond Parasakti and beyond turiya, the single flame of supreme jnana pervading all, the stainless state of sayujya and the bliss-form beyond words. The praise names Murugan, who gave the poet grace to sing the glorious Thiruppugazh of the Kumara whose vel rolled Sura over, and Kathirkamam hill in Ilam, where black monkeys tear open jackfruits and play among plantains and mangoes.
643.nuance: The goal lies past every path the Saiva system names: சரியை, கிரியை and யோகம் fall short, சமயபேதம் cannot come near, and the state is above துரியம். திருப்புகழை ஓதற்கு எனக்கு அருள்வோனே: the book names itself as Murugan's gift. ஈழம் places Kathirkamam in Lanka. சுகசெர்ரு பத்தை is a garble, probably சுகசொரூபத்தை.

644.reading: The poet describes women with heavy pearl-hung breasts, honey-sweet song-like speech, flower-arrow eyes, dark hair and makara earrings, and asks whether he, the lustful man caught in them, will come to forget even the feet that made him forget desire. The praise names Vishnu who crushed the ten-headed one in the city the sun feared to cross, and Murugan at fierce Kathirkamam on the triangular hill of gems, caught in Valli's feet, waist and spear-like eyes on the millet hill.
644.nuance: The song is built on a mirror: the poet is caught (அகப்பட்ட) by women's eyes, and Murugan ends caught (அகப்பட்ட) by Valli's spear-eyes. ஆசையை மறப்பித்த கால்களை மறக்கைக்கும் வருமோ may instead ask whether he will ever forget his desire; the division is uncertain.

645.reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love: wounded by Madana's flower bow and burned by the full moon above the walls, weeping pearls from both eyes through the night, she is wasting away in deep infatuation, and the speaker asks Murugan to come and give her life. The praise names his jewelled chest that delighted in the hunter girl, his form of gold and ruby, Murugan near to his devotees, the first of release, the hero on the green peacock whose vel broke Sura.
645.nuance: An akam lament in another's voice (இவளை வாழ்விக்க வரவேணும்), not the poet's confession. The torments are the classical ones, Kama's bow and the moon at night, with the tears as pearls (முத்தம்).

646.reading: A short song that judges rather than confesses: those who wander under women's power, who roam without thinking of great austerity, and who do not recite and bow so that evil leaves them will shine in the fire of hell. The praise names Murugan the light of nada, of good qualities, the vel who embraces two women, the Kumara of Sivajnana, the flawless lord of Kathirkamam.
646.nuance: தீநரக மீதில் திகழ்வாரே: 'they will shine in hell's fire' is ironic, the verb of glory used for the damned. The song speaks of others in the third person, unusual in a book of first-person pleas.

647.reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love: tormented by the roaring sea, by the moon that rises burning from the poison of the northern fire, by the sweet raga of the cowherds' bamboo flute and by her mothers' unending scolding, she has come to boundless love, and the speaker asks Murugan to come and embrace her. The praise names the god of Kathirkamam with the matchless vel and the bright peacock, the husband of the one of the sky (Devayanai), who gave the bull-riding Isa the hard word of jnana, and who scattered the demons' world to ash so the gods' world might live.
647.nuance: The sea, moon and flute are the evening torments of separated lovers in classical akam; the cowherd's flute is the Kural's image (1228). அரிய ஞான வாசகத்தை அருள்வோனே is the teaching of Siva, without Om being named. விகட மாதை, 'the bold girl', may describe her daring in love.

648.reading: The poet pictures Yama's messengers coming with the palm leaf, seizing him by the waist-cloth, following him with abuse ('a wicked rogue, a cheat in his infatuation'), striking him with weapons, cutting his flesh and pouring out his dark blood until they say 'lay him on the stake', and asks Murugan to come quickly before him at that hour. The praise names the Kumaresa of Senthil, of Idumban and of Palani, who came to Kathirkamam for devotees to see after standing in thousands of shrines and countless hills, the son of the matted-haired Siva who wears serpent, crescent, vilvam and konrai, the guru who came to rule those who trust him.
648.nuance: Death's men here are torturers rather than a summons: the abuse, the cutting and the stake (கழுமுனை) belong more to pictures of hell than to the deathbed songs. The Kathirkamam shrine is presented as the place Murugan came to after all his other shrines.

649.reading: The poet lists the arts of women who glare with sword-like eyes, sway their breasts, loosen their clothes, laugh, let down their hair, embrace on the bed and bite the lips until shame is gone, and asks whether, caught in the net of these sinners, he must lie diseased on a mat, pale, hungry and thirsty like a dog. The praise names Rama, who killed Tataka with one arrow, guarded the sacrifice and broke the great bow, as uncle; Murugan as guru of the father who plucked Brahma's head and burned Kama; the hero on the peacock that shook the serpent's thousand heads and split the mountain; and the lord with Uma who lives in dharma.
649.nuance: The consequence of lust is disease and degradation in this life (நோய் பிணி கிடத்து பாய்மிசை வெளுத்து), not hell. The closing அருக்கொணா மலை is not Kathirkamam, and may be Thirukkonamalai (see 650).

links.note: Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, wounded by Kama's flowers and burned by the moon, and plead with him for her: 337 asks for his garland, 645 that he come and give her life, adding the tears she weeps as pearls through the night.

The Kural's woman hears the cowherd's flute as the herald of a burning evening and a weapon that kills; in 647 the cowherds' bamboo flute is one of the evening torments, with the sea and the moon, of a girl sick for Murugan.
Both place sayujya past the ordinary states of consciousness: Tirumular calls it reaching the state beyond waking and becoming Siva; 643 sets it above turiya and beyond every path and sect.

637 confesses seeking gifts (பரிசில் தேடி) by calling graceless patrons Meru, the seasonal rain cloud and the wish-tree (மேரு ... பருவ மேக மே தாரு). Tirumular tells the reader to seek (நாடுமின்) the king of the gods, who becomes great wealth like the rain-bearing cloud (பெயற்கொண்டல் போலப் பெருஞ்செல்வம்). The cloud the poet wasted on misers is, in the Tirumanthiram, the Lord's own figure, and seeking is aimed at the right giver.

638 counts the householder's needs, cloth (துகில்), food (கனபானம்), water and clothes, a woman and a house, and says the life goes in vain (உயிர் அவமே போம்). Tirumular's list is the same kind, cloth, rice, oil, necklace, marriage thread and bangles (கூறையும் சோறும் ... வளையலும்), and those who fix on them sink into the pit (ஆறைக் குழியில் அழுந்துகின்றாரே). Both make the household a list of wants and the list itself the trap.

638 begins its list of wants with the body, cloth, food and medicine for its sickness (மெய் உறுநோயை ஒழிக்கப் பரிகாரம்), and ends whirling in the mountain of births (பவகிரிக்குள் சுழல்வேனை). The Kural says that for those set on cutting off birth even the body is too much (உடம்பும் மிகை), so what other ties should they keep? The song shows how the body's needs multiply into a household, the case the Kural cuts off at the root.

639 names Murugan by a single epithet, the one who straightened the Pandya's hump (வழுதி கூன் நிமிர்த்த). 666 tells the whole story: he smeared the holy ash on the Pandya (வழுதி மேல் திருநீறே பூசி), the hump straightened, the leaf went against the stream and the Jains were uprooted. Together they show Sambandar's Madurai miracle claimed as Murugan's own deed, in brief and in full.

The Naladiyar says those who mean to reach the right way (செந்நெறிச் சேர்துமென்பார்) do not embrace the breasts of women who go their own way. 641 says such women bring under passion's power (ராகத்தின் வசமாக) even those already walking the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga (சரியைக்ரியை யோகத்தின் வழிவருக்கு). Read together, the song limits the Naladiyar's confidence: being on the path does not by itself keep one away.

642 tells Siva's burning of the cities as a story in short verbs: he laughed and burned them (சிரித்தார் எரித்தார்), then flayed the elephant and burned Madana. Tirumular says fools say only that he destroyed the three cities (முப்புரம் செற்றனன் என்பர்கள் மூடர்கள்); the three cities are the work of the three impurities (மும்மல காரியம்). The Tirumanthiram supplies the inward reading of the deed the song narrates.

643 asks for a reality that those of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga cannot reach and the divisions of sects cannot approach (சமயபேதத்தினுக்கு அணுகொணா). 907, at Vayalur, asks not to perish in the sectarians' rules nor even in the chariyai, kiriyai and yoga disciplines (சரியைக்ரியா யோக நியமத்தின் மாயாது), but to be given unwavering jnana. Both songs set the Saiva paths themselves below the goal, which reads as the book's settled view, not one song's flourish.

644, on one division, asks whether the lustful man caught in women will forget even the feet that made him forget desire (ஆசையை மறப்பித்த கால்கள்). The Kural tells the reader to cling to the clinging of the one who has none, in order to let clinging go (பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை). Both make holding the Lord the means by which desire is undone; the song's fear is losing that hold. The division of the song's line is uncertain.

646 says those who live in women's power, who wander without thinking of great austerity (மாதவம் எணாமல்), and who do not recite and bow will shine in hell's fire. Tirumular says those who practise false austerity also enter hell (பொய்த்தவஞ் செய்வார் புகுவர் நரகத்து), and that austerity holds only by true knowledge. The Tirumanthiram adds a condition the song leaves out: neglecting tapas leads to hell, but so does tapas without jnana.

648 pictures Yama's messengers (நமனுடைய தூதர்) coming with the palm leaf, abusing, cutting and putting the man on the stake, and begs Murugan to come quickly at that hour. Tirumular states as done what the song begs for: the guru kept away the band of Yama's messengers (தவிரவைத்தான் நமன் தூதுவர் கூட்டம்) from his devotees and ended the sorrow of birth. The plea and the assurance use the same figure.

In 648 Yama's men seize the sinner by the waist-cloth before abusing him, cut his flesh and lay him on the stake. In Tirumular's verse on meat-eating, Yama's messengers (இயமன்றன் தூதுவர்) seize the eaters in sight of all, fling them on their backs into fire-mouthed hell and break them. Both draw the messengers as torturers, not only summoners, which places the song's deathbed scene in the imagery of hell.

649 follows a man through women's arts to the bed and then to disease, lying pale, hungry and thirsty on a mat (நோய்பிணி கிடத்து பாய்மிசை வெளுத்து). Tirumular says that with the yoga by which the bindu does not leave, even the joining of two bodies is Siva's pleasure, while fools embrace women without ending infatuation (மோகங் கெட முயங்கார் மூடர்). The pairing limits the song's verdict: the ruin it shows is the fool's union taken in infatuation (மால்கொடு), not union as such, on Tirumular's account.

source_issues: Song 643: unflagged garble சுகசெர்ரு பத்தை (line 136), probably சுகசொரூபத்தை.
Song 649: it closes on அருக்கொணாமலை rather than Kathirkamam; it may belong under Thirukkonamalai (chapter 77), whose song 650 names திருக்கொணாமலை.
